headline: Kepler Computing, a US start-up backed by Intel's venture arm, says it aims to begin producing a lower-energy replacement for high-bandwidth memory in 2027.
score_reason: Kept at the pool level: an ambitious product plan resting on the company's own claims.
importance_line: If it works, AI data centres could get memory that moves more data for the same power and the memory shortage could ease, which would matter to cloud and chip companies, but the performance figures are Kepler's own, the key material is undisclosed and it has named no customers.
source: EE Times, as relayed by IndexBox
summary: EE Times reports, as relayed by IndexBox, that Kepler Computing, a San Jose start-up backed by Intel Capital, intends to start producing memory in 2027 as a lower-power alternative to high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked memory placed beside AI processors, and says it moves five to ten times more data per watt of power than HBM. These are the company's own claims: it declined to reveal its key ferroelectric material, named no customer or partner besides GlobalFoundries, its manufacturing partner and an investor, and says all its 2027 capacity is already allocated.
notes: EE Times page blocked here (HTTP 000); text read at IndexBox, which summarises the EE Times interviews, so the url is the EE Times link and the facts come from the IndexBox relay. Funding and stealth-mode date from WIRED, 9 Sep 2026. Company claims, not independently tested.
